title: Honi and the carob tree
hookLine: Honi's carob tree again: what will grow after you? (Talmud, Taanit 23a)
carry: as others planted for me, i plant for others
last: A LIFE PRESSED INTO A LINE.

lines: A MAN PLANTING A CAROB TREE.
cards: A man is walking along a road and sees someone on his knees in the dirt, planting a carob tree. The walker stops and asks how long it will take before the tree bears fruit. Seventy years, says the planter.
The walker asks the obvious next question: are you so sure you'll live another seventy years?

The walker is Honi, a sage the Talmud remembers in the tractate Taanit, and this may not be the first time you've met him on this path. His story comes back with a new question: what will grow after you?

teach.h: AS MY ANCESTORS PLANTED FOR ME
teach.b: First, the planter's answer. In the Talmud's telling, he says, more or less: I found the world with carob trees in it. As my ancestors planted for me, so I plant for my children.
He isn't planting for himself. He's paying forward a gift he never saw being given.
Second, Honi sleeps. Honi sits down to eat, sleep comes over him, and a rock formation closes around him so that no one sees him. He sleeps for seventy years.
When he wakes, he sees a man gathering carobs from that same tree, and asks: are you the one who planted it? The man answers: I'm his grandson.
Third, an ending that isn't sweet. Honi goes home and to the house of study, and nobody believes he is who he says. No one gives him the honor he was used to.
In his loneliness he asks for death, and he dies. Some readers hear the two halves together: a tree can outlive its planter, and a person still needs companions while they're alive.
Fourth, what the dead leave planted. After a week of grief, the story turns the question around.
The people we've lost planted things we still eat from: a recipe, a way of giving thanks at the table, a habit of showing up, a garden, a joke the family still tells.
And the living can plant too, things whose fruit they won't be around to taste.

how: Some people answer a death by planting: a memorial tree, a scholarship, a garden bed, or simply passing on a recipe or skill the person taught them, so that something keeps growing after the loss.

o: doing good now whose fruit you may never taste
waiting patiently until the time is right to begin
saving money now so you can enjoy it when you retire

games.q: who's who on Honi's road — tap the pairs.

s: in the story, the planter expects to eat the carobs himself
he plants for his children, as his ancestors planted for him.
Honi wakes to find the planter's grandson gathering carobs
he asks, and the man says he's the grandson.
the story ends with Honi welcomed home with honor

games.q: you're the planter. a stranger says you'll never live to eat this tree's fruit. what do you say?
o: my ancestors planted for me, so I plant for my children.
then I'll sell the tree before it grows.
games.why: that's the planter's answer in the Talmud: he found the world with carob trees in it, planted by others.

practice: Bring to mind one thing someone before you planted that you still live from, a recipe, a saying, a skill they taught you, an actual tree, and give them a moment of thanks in whatever way is yours.
Then let one small thing come to mind that could outlast this week, maybe this life: a seed in a pot, a letter for a child to open later, a kindness made into a habit.

wordCard.voice: Plant for later: doing something now whose fruit you may never taste, as others once did for you. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew for carob, the tree in Honi's story.

carryVoice: Your line: as others planted for me, i plant for others. Someone once did it for you, long before you knew. More tomorrow.
